source.title: Classification of Finite Groups: Recent Developements and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Determine all groups of order 1024 up to isomorphism by completing the still-incomplete classification of finite groups of that order. The problem includes both finishing the remaining determination work and, if possible, developing new computational tools that make the required calculations feasible with moderate rather than massive computing power.

evidence.quote: Problem 4 Complete the determination of the groups of order 1024. This problem can perhaps be solved by a straightforward application of the available algorithms using massive computer power. Burrell [ 9] has done a signiﬁcant part of this. It would be interesting to develop new tools that make this computation feasible even with moderate computing power.

accepted.question_text: Determine, up to isomorphism, the finite groups whose order has at most five prime factors, extending the existing complete classification for the case of at most four prime factors. An especially important part of the problem is whether this extension can be achieved by symbolic computation rather than only by case distinctions and hand calculations, so that the resulting method is more efficient.
accepted.context_brief: orders with at most five prime factors

evidence.quote: Problem 5 Determine the groups whose order factorizes into at most 5 primes. This would extend the work by Dietrich et al. [ 15] which has been achieved by case distinctions and hand calculations. It would be particularly interesting if the posed problem could be solved in a different way using symbolic computations, as this would make the solution more efﬁcient.

accepted.question_text: Determine, and explicitly list up to isomorphism, the groups of order p^n · q where p and q are distinct primes and n ≤ 7. Existing work counts such groups only for n ≤ 5 without listing them, so the problem is to make those arguments constructive enough to produce explicit lists and then extend the classification from n = 5 to the harder cases n = 6 and n = 7, preferably using symbolic calculations because the classifications of groups of order p^6 and p^7 are increasingly complicated.

accepted.question_text: Determine all groups of order p^8, for a prime p, up to isomorphism. The paper describes this as a highly challenging classification problem and indicates that any successful solution should rely on computational methods together with symbolic computation.

evidence.quote: Problem 7 Determine the groups of order p 8. This seems a highly challenging problem and its solution should deﬁnitely be based on computational methods and symbolic computations.
